children: East Africa’s costly cross-border transaction costs could benefit from mass uptake of payment solutions available, experts say, offering hope on a longstanding barrier to trade and remittances in the region.

The World Bank estimates that sending money from one digital wallet to another across borders can cost up to 35 percent in East Africa, one of the highest costs globally, due to insufficient payment rail infrastructure, and low margins.

While integrating digital instant payment systems across the region remains a work in progress, several fintechs and banks have stepped up to fill the vacuum with different solutions, but even they are struggling to offer cross-border payment options cheaply.

Experts contend that without a common regional instant payment system, available options can be affordable only if there is mass adoption, enough to spread fixed costs of providing the services across multiple users and maintain the platform’s profitability.

Although technology can shorten payment chains and eliminate some of the intermediaries that have traditionally added to the cost, without sufficient transaction volumes, there is little incentive for providers to make those services cheaper.
This has been seen in major remittance corridors to Africa.

Generally, Africa remains the world’s most expensive region for sending remittances, with the average cost standing at 8.2 percent in the quarter to March, more than twice the global target of at most three percent.

Yet some of the cheapest corridors are those with large transaction volumes. Sending money from the United States to Nigeria now costs less than three percent, while the UK-Kenya corridor averages about 3.9 percent.

Experts say this is because large markets attract more providers, allowing them to compete on price. Some fintechs have even abandoned transaction fees altogether, relying instead on small foreign-exchange margins, a model that only works when large amounts of money are moving through the system.“The only way this business model can be sustainable is if there are large volumes of money being moved,” Vincent Aberi, East Africa growth manager at LemFi, said in a past interview with The EastAfrican. “We don’t charge transaction fees. Meaning that we can only make money from the forex margins, which are very small. So it can only make sense in high-volume corridors.”Beyond remittances, other cross-border payment options, like Kenya’s emerging payment solutions for foreign visitors, are also banking on increased volumes to reduce costs.

Platforms like Tourist Tap and Cashia, though convenient, cost up to 5 percent for foreigners seeking to pay into mobile money without first getting a local Sim card. This is nearly five times the average cost of local mobile money and bank-to-bank instant payment platforms.

That matters because the cost of a payment is not determined by technology alone. Every additional intermediary, whether a card provider, bank, fintech or another service provider, can add to the final bill.“If you put in place efficient payment systems, we can also reduce the number… of intermediaries and then we can work on the cost,” Mr Akogbeto said.

However, reducing the number of intermediaries is only part of the equation. The remaining participants still need to make enough money from the system to keep it running. Higher transaction volumes provide that room.
